o.A: Hand hygiene is not required after leaving because the nurse did not touch the patient directly.
o.B: Hand hygiene is indicated after touching equipment in the patient’s immediate surroundings, even without direct patient contact.
o.C: Hand hygiene is needed after equipment contact when the device is visibly soiled, but routine contact alone does not create an indication.
o.D: Hand hygiene can be deferred until the next patient-care task because no body-fluid exposure occurred.

items.s: A nurse enters a room, adjusts an IV pump in the patient’s immediate surroundings without touching the patient, and then leaves. When is hand hygiene indicated?
items.r: CDC hand-hygiene guidance includes performing hand hygiene after touching a patient’s immediate surroundings or equipment, even when the patient was not directly touched.

o.C: Review operations with staff and address modifiable drivers such as staffing, workload, scheduling, administrative burden, safety, and support.

o.A: Assess the client, use required clinical and safety reporting channels, document factual care, and continue indicated monitoring.
o.B: Withhold reporting unless the client later develops an injury or measurable adverse effect from the error.
o.C: Complete the causal investigation independently before informing the care team or the organization’s safety process.
o.D: Document routine medication administration and continue observation; formal event reporting can wait unless symptoms or injury emerge.

items.s: A medication error reaches a client, but immediate assessment shows no apparent injury. Which nursing response best supports patient safety?
items.r: The 2026 NCSBN test plan includes acknowledging and documenting practice errors and near misses, reporting incidents/events, intervening or escalating safety concerns, and evaluating the client’s response. A no-harm outcome does not eliminate the need for assessment and required reporting.

o.A: Use equal patient counts as the main rule even when acuity and required nursing care differ substantially.
o.B: Match client acuity and care needs with nurse competence, workload, and available resources rather than relying on numbers alone.
o.C: Give the most complex clients to the least experienced nurse so difficult assignments are distributed evenly.
o.D: Base assignments mainly on room location because geographic efficiency outweighs differences in acuity.

items.s: A charge nurse assigns one RN a client needing frequent complex wound care, another with unstable hemodynamics, and two stable clients. Which principle should guide the assignment?
items.r: The current NCSBN test plan directs nurses to prioritize care based on acuity and to make assignments/delegations according to client needs and personnel competency while considering available resources. Equal numbers alone do not establish a safe workload.

o.D: Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia because hypertension first appeared during this pregnancy.

items.s: A pregnant client at 34 weeks with intact membranes develops sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. The fetal heart tracing is reassuring. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
items.r: ACOG describes placenta previa as a cause of later-pregnancy vaginal bleeding that often occurs without pain. Placental abruption more often includes abdominal or back pain. Intact membranes and a reassuring fetal tracing make vasa previa less consistent with the complete presentation, though any third-trimester bleeding requires urgent obstetric evaluation.
